common_name: Tondo di Paestum Artichoke (Carciofo di Paestum IGP)
scientific_name: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Tondo di Paestum'

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant, or set out rooted offshoots in spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Established stools flower over a long season in mild coastal climates, so harvest the central bud first and keep cutting side buds as they tighten.

directions: Tondo di Paestum is the traditional round-headed artichoke landrace grown on the coastal plain around Paestum and Battipaglia in Campania, Italy, where it carries IGP protected status for its tender, compact, violet-tinged green heads harvested from late winter into spring. The mild coastal Mediterranean winters of its home region allow continuous bud production over several months, with the earliest central buds valued for their uniform roundness and the smaller side buds suited to braising or preserving in oil. Plants are traditionally kept as perennial stools and increased by dividing rooted offshoots rather than grown fresh from seed each year, which preserves the landrace's characteristic head shape and timing. Give it deep, well-drained coastal soil and full sun, and mulch crowns if a rare hard frost threatens.
sources: Consorzio di Tutela del Carciofo di Paestum IGP

common_name: Sardinian Spiny Artichoke (Carciofo Spinoso di Sardegna DOP)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant, or set out rooted suckers in spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Sardinia's mild, dry-summer climate suits long-lived perennial stools that are increased by division rather than annual reseeding.

directions: Spinoso di Sardegna is Sardinia's DOP-protected spiny artichoke, grown mainly on the island's southern plains where mild winters and sandy coastal soils support heavy perennial production of elongated, sharply spined, violet-green heads. The spines mark the outer bracts but not the tender heart and inner bract bases, which Sardinian cooks favor raw and thinly sliced with olive oil and pecorino, or stewed whole with fava beans in the classic spring dish carciofi e fave. Plants are long-lived perennials traditionally increased from rooted suckers rather than seed, forming dense clumps that remain productive for many years with periodic division. Full sun and deep, well-drained soil with a dry summer rest between crops suit this variety best.
sources: Regione Sardegna — Carciofo Spinoso di Sardegna DOP Disciplinare

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant, or set out rooted offshoots in spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Mild Adriatic winters around Brindisi allow harvest from autumn through spring on established stools.

directions: Brindisino is the IGP-recognized artichoke grown around Brindisi in coastal Puglia, where mild Adriatic winters allow an extended harvest from autumn through spring. Heads are medium-sized, rounded, and tightly closed around a mild, tender heart that local cooks favor for stewing with potatoes and peas or braising whole in olive oil and garlic. Like other southern Italian landraces it is grown as a long-lived perennial and increased by dividing offshoots from established stools rather than annual reseeding. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water through dry summer stretches to keep crowns productive.
sources: Regione Puglia — Carciofo Brindisino IGP Disciplinare

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant, or set out rooted offshoots in spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Calabria's mild hill-country winters suit long-lived perennial stools maintained by division.

directions: Mammola is a traditional Calabrian artichoke landrace associated with the town of Mammola in the province of Reggio Calabria, listed as a regional traditional product for its spineless, violet-green, elongated heads. It is valued locally for a tender heart with less fibrous bract tissue to trim than spinier types, which makes the smaller side buds suitable for eating raw or lightly cooked. Grown as a long-lived perennial in Calabria's mild hill country, it is traditionally increased by dividing rooted offshoots from mature clumps rather than from seed. Give it full sun and deep, well-drained soil, and divide crowded clumps every few years to maintain vigor.
sources: Regione Calabria — Prodotti Agroalimentari Tradizionali (PAT) List

scientific_name: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Violetto di Sant'Erasmo'

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant, or set out rooted offshoots in spring; in zone 8 plant March–April. The prized castraura, the plant's small first central bud, is removed early to redirect vigor into later side buds.

directions: Violetto di Sant'Erasmo is grown on Sant'Erasmo, an island in the Venice lagoon, where the sandy, lightly saline soil and lagoon microclimate are credited with the exceptional tenderness of this violet-tinged artichoke, recognized as a Slow Food Presidium product. The most prized harvest is the castraura, the plant's small, tender first central bud removed in spring to redirect vigor into the larger side buds that follow, and it is traditionally eaten raw, thinly sliced. Plants are maintained as perennial stools and increased by dividing rooted offshoots, consistent with lagoon market-garden tradition rather than seed propagation. Grow in full sun in loose, well-drained, sandy soil, and where lagoon salt-air conditions do not apply, provide winter mulch for crown protection.
sources: Slow Food Presidia — Carciofo Violetto di Sant'Erasmo
